  "title": "Latent-Distribution Candidate Selection for Frozen World Action Models: OOD Consistency Scoring and Action-Latent Value Learning",
  "core_problem": "Pretrained WAMs generate a single action trajectory at inference and provide no mechanism to compare candidate futures. Adding planning capability currently requires one of three costly interventions: (1) full fine-tuning of the video model on robot demos (Cosmos Policy, ICLR 2026: 384–3,072 H100-hours); (2) training a separate action-conditioned world model alongside the frozen policy (GPC, RAL 2025); or (3) architectural co-design or RL loops (H-WM, GigaBrain RAMP, WAV). Fast-WAM (arXiv 2603.16666) demonstrates that action-only inference achieves 97.6% on LIBERO (Table 2) and 91.8% on RoboTwin (Table 1) at 190ms, motivating candidate generation from frozen WAM action-only inference rather than expensive video rollouts.

The test-time candidate selection literature (2024–2026) has established three tiers of action representation for scoring candidates, with each tier providing increasingly structured quality-discriminative geometry:

**Tier 1 — Cartesian action space**: V-GPS (arXiv 2410.13816, CoRL 2024) trains a Q-function via offline RL (Cal-QL) on raw 7-dimensional Cartesian action vectors concatenated with ResNet-34 image embeddings, scoring K=50 candidates from frozen generalist policies (Octo, RT-1X, OpenVLA) and achieving +82.8% relative improvement on real-robot tasks — establishing that value-function re-ranking of frozen policies works in Cartesian+image space. KDPE (arXiv 2508.10511, CoRL 2025) applies kernel density estimation to Cartesian action trajectories (end-effector position, SO(3)-orientation, gripper state) from Diffusion Policy to filter multimodal outputs, generating N=100 candidates; achieves 88.2% vs. 85% on RoboMimic/MimicGen. Critical KDPE finding: KDPE-OOD (selecting the most out-of-distribution trajectory) performs dramatically worse than KDPE on the ToolHang precision task (KDPE-OOD-C: 7% vs. KDPE-C: 76%, Table 1) — confirming that in-distribution selection is the correct direction for LOC. Both Tier 1 methods operate on low-dimensional raw action representations with no latent structure encoding physical plausibility beyond what is captured by pixel-level image embeddings.

**Tier 2 — VLA action tokens**: MG-Select (arXiv 2510.05681, ICLR 2026) uses KL-divergence from a masked unconditional VLA distribution as a training-free confidence signal, achieving 168% relative improvement on RoboCasa pick-and-place. RoVer (arXiv 2510.10975, ICLR 2026) trains a 0.2B Process Reward Model that scores candidates from frozen VLAs. Both operate on VLA action tokens from architectures trained on language-action pairs without joint video-action pretraining, lacking the video-physics co-regularization that structures WAM action latents.

**Adjacent latent-space methods (not candidate selection)**: Latent Policy Barrier (LPB, arXiv 2508.05941, 2025) measures Euclidean distance in visual observation latent space (frozen visual encoder from base diffusion policy) to the nearest expert demo state as an OOD signal, then performs gradient-based steering of the action denoising process at runtime when OOD is detected — using a separate dynamics model trained on expert plus suboptimal rollout data. Latent Policy Steering (LPS, arXiv 2507.13340, 2025) trains a value function in world model latent state space (Dreamer v3) on expert plus policy-rollout states, using optical flow as an embodiment-agnostic action representation, achieving 70% relative improvement with 30–50 demos on real-world tasks. Neither approach answers the question we ask: do WAM action latents z_a, shaped by joint video-action pretraining, enable pre-execution candidate scoring without rollout data or observation-space engineering?

**Tier 3 — WAM action latents** (this paper's domain): UWM and DreamZero generate action latents z_a from joint video-action diffusion pretraining. Cosmos Policy (ICLR 2026) implements Best-of-N in its planning mode by generating B candidates and scoring each via a fine-tuned value function — but requires rollout fine-tuning (1,536 H100-hours for RoboCasa) because demonstration-only training 'cannot correctly predict failure states.'

The central unanswered question — which Tier 1 and Tier 2 approaches cannot answer, and which LPB/LPS do not address — is: (1) Do WAM action latents z_a, regularized by joint video-action pretraining, form a latent success distribution that is more structured and separable from failure regimes than VLA action tokens (Tier 2) or Cartesian action representations (Tier 1), enabling lightweight OOD-based candidate scoring without any rollout data? (2) Does operating in WAM latent space alone (without needing an image at inference) enable a more compact, efficient quality discriminator than Tier 1 methods that require both image and action? These questions are grounded in the FAIL-Detect (arXiv 2503.08558, RSS 2025) finding that OOD detection on success-only demonstrations reliably identifies failures — but have not been applied to WAM action latents or to pre-execution candidate selection.

Important caveat on z_a geometry: In action-only inference (video timestep = T), video tokens are at full noise and provide no inference-time conditioning. The quality-discriminative structure of z_a is therefore a training-time property — joint pretraining causes the model to learn representations where z_a co-varies with visual futures, but whether this geometry persists as a success/failure discriminator when video is absent at inference is not proven a priori. Step 1 (LOC diagnostic) is the first empirical test. If H1 fails (AUC < 0.55), LOC reports a negative result and Value MLP becomes the sole primary contribution.

The companion question of whether video denoising error (as opposed to latent OOD scoring) is a reliable zero-training signal is answered negatively by Cosmos Policy's own finding and by EVA (arXiv 2603.17808), which demonstrates an 'executability gap' showing that visual coherence does not predict task success.

No existing work demonstrates Best-of-N candidate selection using WAM action latents' distributional structure — either zero-training (OOD scoring) or lightweight-trained (value MLP) — without modifying any WAM weights or requiring rollout data for the zero-training path. The three-tier hierarchy predicts that z_a offers the richest quality-discriminative geometry for frozen-policy candidate selection, a hypothesis this paper tests empirically.",
  "opportunity": "UWM's independent per-modality diffusion timestep architecture (RSS 2025) natively supports action-only inference (video timestep = T, action timestep = 0), producing action latents z_a jointly pretrained with video. This creates two complementary WAM-specific approaches to candidate selection:

**Method 1 — Latent OOD Consistency Scoring (LOC, zero weight updates)**: Encode LIBERO-90 success demonstrations through frozen UWM in action-only mode to obtain a reference distribution {z_a^success}. Fit a lightweight density estimator — KNN-based nonconformity score (k=10) or Gaussian Mixture Model (k≤5 components) — on {z_a^success}. At inference, sample B=4–8 action-only candidates from frozen UWM, obtain latents {z_{a,1}, ..., z_{a,B}}, and score each: S_LOC(z_{a,i}) = −log p̂(z_{a,i}) (nonconformity score). Select a_{i*} = argmin_i S_LOC(z_{a,i}) (most in-distribution candidate). Total inference overhead: B × ~5ms = 20–40ms for B=4–8. Cost: ~30–60 minutes to fit density estimator on encoded latents; no WAM weight updates.

Theoretical basis: (1) FAIL-Detect (RSS 2025) proves that OOD detection on success-only demonstration data reliably detects policy failures — the success-demo distribution implicitly excludes failure modes; (2) KDPE (CoRL 2025) demonstrates in Cartesian action space that selecting the most IN-distribution trajectory improves performance, while KDPE-OOD collapses performance on the ToolHang precision task (KDPE-OOD-C: 7% vs. KDPE-C: 76%) — validating the in-distribution selection direction for LOC; (3) z_a from joint video-action pretraining is hypothesized to encode physical plausibility in a tighter quality-discriminative geometry than both Cartesian action space (KDPE, V-GPS) and VLA action tokens. **Inference-time caveat**: In action-only mode, video tokens are at full noise (timestep T) — this quality-discriminative geometry is a training-time property of the learned weights, not an inference-time video conditioning effect. Step 1 empirically tests whether this training-time property persists as a quality signal without video input. LOC is reported as a negative result if AUC < 0.55.

Key differentiation from KDPE and V-GPS (Tier 1 methods): (a) density estimation in WAM action latent space z_a, not Cartesian action space (position/orientation/gripper) or 7D delta actions; (b) success-demonstrations-only reference distribution establishing a quality anchor, not all training data (KDPE) or a separately collected offline RL dataset (V-GPS); (c) no image required at inference — z_a encodes visual-physical context from joint pretraining, unlike V-GPS which concatenates a ResNet-34 image embedding with the raw action for every candidate; (d) B=4–8 candidates vs. KDPE's N=100 and V-GPS's K=50. LOC implements success-mode latent selection; KDPE implements Cartesian-space all-data-mode selection; V-GPS implements offline-RL Q-function scoring in Cartesian+image space — these are mechanistically distinct quality signals across the three representational tiers.

Differentiation from MG-Select: LOC scores membership in the success demonstration distribution (latent OOD density); MG-Select measures KL divergence of task-conditioned output from masked unconditional distribution (action-space distributional uncertainty).

Differentiation from Latent Policy Barrier (LPB, arXiv 2508.05941): LPB operates in visual observation latent space (frozen visual encoder from base diffusion policy), measures Euclidean distance to nearest expert demo observation embedding, and performs gradient-based runtime steering of action denoising when out-of-distribution — requiring a separate dynamics model trained on expert plus suboptimal rollout data. LOC operates in WAM action latent space z_a (not observation latents), uses KNN/GMM density estimation on success demos, and scores B candidates PRE-EXECUTION rather than steering during execution — exploiting WAM joint-pretraining geometry unavailable to observation-space methods and requiring zero rollout data.

Note on Cosmos Policy planning mode: Cosmos Policy also implements Best-of-N — generates B actions, predicts future states and values, executes the highest-value action. However, (a) requires fine-tuning a value function on rollout data (1,536 H100-hours for RoboCasa) because demonstration-only training 'cannot correctly predict failure states'; (b) 15 total forward passes per candidate. LOC requires zero rollout data, zero weight updates, and ~5ms per candidate.

**Method 2 — Action-Latent Value MLP (≤40 H100-hours training)**: A 3-layer MLP trained on WAM action latents z_a from LIBERO-90 success demonstrations AND explicitly collected failure trajectories scores each candidate via V(z_{a,i}) ∈ [0,1]. Hard argmax Best-of-N is the primary result. Key hypothesis: z_a regularized by joint video-action pretraining is more linearly separable between success and failure regimes than raw action outputs, VLA action tokens, or Cartesian representations — enabling a simpler, image-free quality discriminator.

Differentiation from V-GPS (CoRL 2024): V-GPS trains a Q-function via offline RL (Cal-QL) on (image observation, raw 7D Cartesian action) pairs — requiring both a ResNet-34 image encoder and the raw action candidate at inference; our Value MLP trains on WAM action latents z_a alone via binary success/failure supervision — no image required at inference because z_a already encodes visual-physical context from joint pretraining. V-GPS validates the value re-ranking paradigm in Cartesian+image space for VLA-family policies; our Value MLP asks whether WAM latent space provides a more compact, image-free quality signal with stronger success/failure linear separability. Additionally, V-GPS uses sparse binary rewards + Cal-QL offline RL; our Value MLP uses direct binary classification supervision, making it trainable in <5 H100-hours vs. V-GPS's offline RL pipeline. Other differentiations: (a) vs. WAV — WAV trains a trajectory value module as a new architectural component from scratch; Value MLP is plug-in-compatible with any pretrained WAM; (b) vs. RoVer — RoVer requires a 0.2B PRM trained on process labels; Value MLP uses a 3-layer MLP trained on binary success/failure labels; (c) vs. Cosmos Policy — requires 1,536 H100-hours rollout fine-tuning; Value MLP requires ≤40 H100-hours.

Differentiation from Latent Policy Steering (LPS, arXiv 2507.13340): LPS trains a value function in world model latent state space (Dreamer v3 architecture) using optical flow as an embodiment-agnostic action representation, requiring both expert demonstration states and policy-rollout states for training (so the value function sees distribution-shifted states). Our Value MLP trains on WAM-specific action latents z_a from joint video-action pretraining — not observation/state latents — and requires only binary success/failure labels from collected failures without policy-visit rollout data, testing whether WAM joint pretraining creates a more linearly separable latent geometry that enables a 3-layer image-free MLP to match discriminative power achieved by observation-space value functions.

**Comparison of LOC vs. Value MLP is itself a central contribution**: Their empirical comparison characterizes when WAM latent OOD scoring is sufficient versus when labeled training adds necessary discriminative power — and whether this latent-space approach outperforms Tier 1 (Cartesian + image, V-GPS) and Tier 2 (VLA token distributional uncertainty, MG-Select) methods.

**Mandatory RoboCasa baseline validation before committing to targets**: World2Act (arXiv 2603.10422, March 2026) reports UWM achieving 60.8% on RoboCasa using 1,000 real demonstration fine-tuning. Since UWM was trained only on DROID data and has not been fine-tuned on RoboCasa tasks, the frozen UWM baseline (no RoboCasa demos) is expected to be substantially lower — likely 10–25%. Primary performance target: ≥10pp absolute improvement over the measured frozen baseline.",
  "landscape": "Cosmos Policy (arXiv 2601.16163, ICLR 2026) is the primary comparison point for absolute performance. Fully fine-tunes Cosmos-Predict2-2B on robot demos (384 H100-hours ALOHA, 1,536 RoboCasa, 3,072 LIBERO). Achieves 98.5% LIBERO and 67.1% RoboCasa. Its planning mode implements Best-of-N candidate selection: generates B candidate actions, predicts future states (3 queries to world model) and values (5 queries to value function per future state, 15 total predictions per action), and executes via majority-mean aggregation. Key distinction: Cosmos Policy's authors explicitly state that demo-only training 'cannot correctly predict failure states' — rollout fine-tuning is required for the planning value function. LOC requires zero rollout data and zero weight updates; Value MLP requires ≤40 H100-hours vs. 1,536 H100-hours.

V-GPS (arXiv 2410.13816, CoRL 2024) — CRITICAL PRIOR WORK for Value MLP. 'Steering Your Generalists: Improving Robotic Foundation Models via Value Guidance.' Trains a Q-function via offline RL (Cal-QL) on sparse binary rewards from demonstration data; architecture: ResNet-34 image encoder with FiLM language conditioning, 7-dimensional Cartesian action vector concatenated with image embedding passed through 2-layer MLP to predict scalar Q-value. At inference, samples K=50 action candidates from frozen generalist policies (Octo-small, Octo-base, Octo-small-1.5, RT-1X, OpenVLA) and re-ranks by Q-value. Achieves +82.8% relative improvement on real-robot 6-task benchmark (Octo-small-1.5 baseline: 24%, V-GPS: 44%). Key differentiations from our Value MLP: (a) V-GPS operates in Cartesian+image space — requires both ResNet-34 image embedding AND raw 7D action candidate at every inference call; our Value MLP operates on WAM z_a alone — no image needed at inference because z_a encodes visual-physical context from joint pretraining; (b) V-GPS uses offline RL (Cal-QL) training pipeline; our Value MLP uses binary success/failure classification, trainable in <5 H100-hours; (c) V-GPS applies to generalist VLA policies (Cartesian action outputs without video-physics pretraining); our Value MLP exploits WAM-specific latent geometry from joint video-action pretraining. V-GPS validates the paradigm (value re-ranking of frozen policies works) in Tier 1 (Cartesian+image space); our paper asks whether Tier 3 (WAM latent space) provides a more discriminative, image-free signal.

KDPE (arXiv 2508.10511, CoRL 2025) — CRITICAL PRIOR WORK. Applies manifold-aware KDE to Cartesian action trajectories (end-effector position/SO(3)-orientation/gripper) from Diffusion Policy; generates N=100 candidates; achieves 88.2% vs. 85% on RoboMimic/MimicGen (CNN-based). CRITICAL FINDING: KDPE-OOD (selecting most out-of-distribution trajectory) collapses performance on the ToolHang precision task to 7% (KDPE-OOD-C) vs. 76% for KDPE-C — a dramatic 69pp gap that provides strong empirical grounding for LOC's argmin selection direction. Differentiates from LOC: (a) Cartesian action space vs. WAM action latent space; (b) all training data vs. success-only reference; (c) no WAM-specific joint pretraining regularization; (d) N=100 candidates vs. LOC's B=4–8.

World2Act (arXiv 2603.10422, March 2026) — post-training framework achieving ~66% on RoboCasa using 50 real + 50 imagined demos; reports UWM achieves 60.8% on RoboCasa with 1,000-demo fine-tuning (confirming frozen UWM baseline is ~10–25%); differentiation: World2Act requires contrastive post-training to align VLA latents; LOC exploits WAM alignment inherited from joint pretraining.

Fast-WAM (arXiv 2603.16666) — CRITICAL FRAMING: 97.6% LIBERO-avg (Table 2) and 91.8% RoboTwin (Table 1) at 190ms without video; single trajectory only; our method uses same action-only inference for candidate generation and adds LOC selection at B × 5ms overhead.

RoVer (arXiv 2510.10975, ICLR 2026) — CRITICAL PRIOR WORK: generates B VLA candidates, trains 0.2B PRM; differentiation: requires 0.2B model training vs. LOC's zero training and Value MLP's 3-layer MLP; VLA action tokens lack video-physics regularization.

Verifier-free Test-Time Sampling / MG-Select (arXiv 2510.05681, ICLR 2026) — CRITICAL PRIOR WORK: training-free KL-from-masked-distribution scoring for frozen VLAs; 168% relative improvement on RoboCasa pick-and-place; differentiation: MG-Select measures action-space distributional uncertainty, LOC measures latent OOD membership relative to success demo distribution.

World-Value-Action (WAV) Model (arXiv 2604.14732, April 2026) — trajectory value module requiring training from scratch, new architectural component; iterative latent-space inference concentrating probability mass on high-value trajectories. LIBERO results (Table 1): Spatial 100.0%, Object 98.6%, Goal 94.4%, Long 98.1% (~97.8% arithmetic average across 4 splits); 75.6% real-world average (Figure 2, dual-arm Piper robot, 15 trials per task). Note: WAV's LIBERO evaluation covers 4 benchmark splits but does not include LIBERO-90; our primary evaluation uses LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa. Differentiation: WAV trains value and world model jointly from scratch (architectural co-design); our method leaves all WAM weights frozen and is plug-in-compatible with any pretrained WAM.

Being-H0.7 (arXiv 2605.00078, May 2026) — concurrent WAM achieving 99.2% on LIBERO average via latent prior-posterior alignment between egocentric video pretraining and robot action finetuning. Not a candidate selection paper — uses a single-trajectory policy architecture rather than Best-of-N scoring. Cited to contextualize the near-saturation LIBERO performance level for strong recent WAMs; our method targets RoboCasa as the meaningful discrimination benchmark.

Latent Policy Barrier (LPB, arXiv 2508.05941, 2025) — uses Euclidean distance in visual observation latent space (frozen visual encoder from base diffusion policy) to nearest expert demo state as OOD signal; at inference, monitors OOD score and applies gradient-based action denoising corrections at runtime when the predicted state leaves the expert distribution; uses a separate dynamics model trained on expert plus suboptimal rollout data. Differentiation from LOC: LPB operates on observation latents (not WAM action latents z_a), performs runtime execution-time steering (not pre-execution candidate selection), and requires a dynamics model trained on rollout data rather than zero rollout data. LOC exploits WAM joint-pretraining geometry unavailable to observation-space methods and scores B candidates before execution.

Latent Policy Steering (LPS, arXiv 2507.13340, 2025) — trains a value function in world model latent state space (Dreamer v3 architecture) on expert demonstration states plus policy-rollout states, using optical flow as an embodiment-agnostic action representation; achieves 70% relative improvement with 30–50 target-embodiment demonstrations on real-world tasks and 10.6% average improvement on Robomimic. Differentiation from Value MLP: LPS trains its value function in world model latent state space (not WAM action latents z_a from joint video-action pretraining); requires policy-rollout data (not just binary success/failure from collected failures); uses optical flow rather than WAM z_a. Our Value MLP tests whether WAM joint pretraining creates a more linearly separable action-latent geometry enabling a 3-layer image-free MLP trained only on binary success/failure labels.

Best-of-Q (arXiv 2601.22701, January 2026) — Q-function re-ranking of frozen VLM agents for digital tasks (web/OS control); mechanistically analogous to V-GPS applied to digital agents; not in robot manipulation domain but confirms paradigm generality beyond robotics.

ALT Policy (arXiv 2505.05787, May 2025) — 'Demystifying Diffusion Policies: Action Memorization and Simple Lookup Table Alternatives': demystifies diffusion policies as implicit nearest-neighbor lookup tables, using contrastive image encoder distance in observation latent space as a runtime OOD signal for single-trajectory retrieval. Related to LOC in applying latent-space OOD proximity as a quality signal, but operates in observation (not action) latent space and retrieves a single stored trajectory rather than scoring multi-candidate selections.

UNISafe (arXiv 2505.00779, May 2025) — 'Uncertainty-aware Latent Safety Filters for Avoiding Out-of-Distribution Failures': calibrates a world model's epistemic uncertainty via conformal prediction to detect OOD state predictions, then performs Hamilton-Jacobi reachability in augmented latent+uncertainty space to synthesize a policy-agnostic safety filter. Related to LOC in applying conformal prediction to world-model latents, but targets state-space safety intervention rather than pre-execution action-latent candidate selection for task performance.

VLS (arXiv 2602.03973, February 2026) — 'Steering Pretrained Robot Policies via Vision-Language Models': applies VLM-generated reward gradients to steer frozen diffusion/flow-matching policies' denoising process toward semantically correct behaviors; training-free guidance via language-conditioned reward signals, not latent-space density or value functions. Different mechanism from both LOC and Value MLP; concurrent work.

FAIL-Detect (arXiv 2503.08558, RSS 2025) — SUPPORTING WORK: proves OOD detection on success-only demonstration data reliably detects policy failures; uses flow-based density estimation on distilled policy signals; motivates LOC's use of KNN/GMM density on success demo latents; FAIL-Detect is execution-time monitoring, LOC is pre-execution candidate selection — Step 1 LOC diagnostic is the first empirical test of whether this principle transfers to pre-execution WAM z_a.

EVA (arXiv 2603.17808, 2026) — identifies 'executability gap' showing visually coherent world model rollouts can violate kinematic constraints; supports LOC over PCS: visual denoising error does not predict task success.

WAV: see above. Compose Your Policies! / GPC (arXiv 2510.01068) — training-free convex composition of multiple frozen policy distributions; operates at distribution level, not discrete candidate selection from single WAM. GPC-RANK (arXiv 2502.00622, IEEE RAL 2025): frozen policy + separately trained action-conditioned world model + hard argmax; uses world-model reward prediction for scoring, not WAM action latent OOD. When to Trust Imagination (arXiv 2605.06222, May 2026): FFDC adaptively decides action chunk sizes during single-trajectory execution; orthogonal and combinable.",
  "approach": "Primary backbone: UWM (github.com/WEIRDLabUW/unified-world-model, RSS 2025), whose independent per-modality diffusion timestep architecture supports action-only inference (policy mode: video timestep = T, action timestep = 0). All WAM weights frozen throughout.

**Step 0a — Frozen UWM Baseline Validation on RoboCasa (MANDATORY FIRST STEP)**: Run B=1 frozen UWM action-only inference on 50 episodes of representative RoboCasa tasks (kitchen manipulation subset). Expected baseline: 10–25% (UWM trained on DROID data only; World2Act reports 60.8% with 1,000-demo fine-tuning, confirming frozen baseline is substantially lower). Decision tree: if baseline ≥ 30%, proceed with current framing; if baseline 10–25%, confirm ≥10pp absolute improvement framing. Cost: ~2–3 H100-hours.

**Step 0b — Reference Distribution Encoding for LOC**: Encode LIBERO-90 success demos through frozen UWM in action-only mode to obtain {z_a^success}. Fit density estimators: (a) KNN nonconformity model (k=10, Euclidean distance); (b) GMM (k=3,5 components, full covariance). Split latents 80/20 train/hold-out for AUC evaluation in Step 1. Cost: ~10–15 H100-hours encoding; ~30 minutes fitting density estimator. Steps 0b and 0c can run in parallel after Step 0a completes.

**Step 0c — Failure Demonstration Collection (required for Value MLP)**: (a) Primary negatives: run frozen UWM (B=1) on LIBERO-Long and validated RoboCasa tasks; expected failure rate 30–50% on RoboCasa tasks, 5–15% on LIBERO-Long, yielding 500–2,000 failure trajectories. Cost: 15–20 H100-hours. (b) Synthetic supplement: Gaussian action perturbation (σ ∈ {0.05, 0.1}) on 20% of LIBERO-90 success demos, simulate in MuJoCo, flag truncated episodes as failures. Cost: <1 H100-hour. Combined: balanced 2,000–4,000 positive / 2,000–4,000 negative training set.

**Step 1 — LOC Diagnostic (MANDATORY before main ablation)**: Empirically tests Hypothesis H1: 'WAM joint pretraining creates a latent success distribution where S_LOC(z_a) achieves AUC > 0.60 as a binary success predictor.' Theoretical motivation: FAIL-Detect's principle (OOD on success-only data detects failures) + KDPE's empirical confirmation (KDPE-OOD collapses ToolHang from 76% to 7%, confirming in-distribution selection outperforms outlier selection in Cartesian space). Inference-time caveat: z_a geometry is a training-time property — in action-only inference, video tokens are at full noise (timestep T) providing no inference-time conditioning. We hypothesize that joint training causes z_a to learn quality-discriminative representations even without video input, but Step 1 is the first empirical test of this hypothesis. If H1 fails (AUC < 0.55), LOC reports a negative result.

Protocol: Sample B=16 action-only candidates from frozen UWM on 3 RoboCasa tasks, execute each in simulation (ground-truth success/failure), compute LOC and comparison scores.

LOC metrics: (1) AUC of S_LOC as binary success predictor on held-out demos (target H1: AUC > 0.60); (2) Spearman ρ of S_LOC with success labels (target ρ > 0.3); (3) compare KNN vs. GMM density estimators. Also compute: S_PCS = ||ε − ε_θ(x_{t*}, z_{a,i}, t*)||² for the same candidates, varying t* ∈ {T/4, T/2, 3T/4} (expected to show lower AUC based on Cosmos Policy finding and EVA's executability gap); MG-Select-style KL score as Tier 2 comparison; KDPE-style Cartesian density as Tier 1 comparison baseline.

Expected result: LOC AUC > PCS AUC ≈ MG-Select AUC ≈ KDPE-Cartesian AUC, confirming Tier 3 (WAM latent) is more informative than Tier 1 (Cartesian) and Tier 2 (VLA token distributional uncertainty) methods.

Decision tree: if AUC ≥ 0.60, LOC is primary zero-training method; if LOC 0.55–0.60, both methods reported with LOC as secondary; if LOC < 0.55, LOC reported as negative result with informative comparison.

**Step 2 — Diversity Pilot (combined with LOC diagnostic)**: Same B=16 rollouts measure: pairwise cosine distance of action latents {z_{a,i}} (target mean > 0.05; if lower, increase noise temperature T_noise ∈ {1.5, 2.0}); LOC AUC conditional on latent diversity.

**Step 3 — Value MLP Training**: 3-layer MLP (input: flattened z_a; output: scalar V ∈ [0,1]) trained via binary cross-entropy on balanced success/failure latents from Steps 0b and 0c. Report binary classification accuracy on held-out split (target > 75%). Key distinction from V-GPS: no image input required at inference — z_a encodes visual-physical context from joint pretraining, making the Value MLP an image-free quality discriminator. Cost: ~3–5 H100-hours.

**Step 4 — Inference-Time Best-of-N Planning**: At each planning step, sample B=4–8 action-only trajectories from frozen UWM.

Primary results (two methods):
- LOC selection: a_{i*} = argmin_i S_LOC(z_{a,i}) at best density estimator from diagnostic [zero weight updates, WAM-specific, no image at inference]
- Value MLP selection: a_{i*} = argmax_i V(z_{a,i}) [lightweight training, WAM-specific, no image at inference]

Comparisons (required): V-GPS-style Cartesian Q-function applied to WAM action outputs (Tier 1 baseline); MG-Select-style KL scoring applied to WAM action-only inference (Tier 2 baseline); random selection (B=4–8, sanity check); single-trajectory WAM B=1 (frozen baseline).

Ablation (secondary): (a) PCS denoising error selection at best t* from diagnostic (expected to underperform LOC); (b) soft MPPI w_i ∝ exp(β·V(z_{a,i})) to document action-averaging artifact; (c) action-only z_a vs. full video+action latent for LOC and Value MLP scoring.

# Cortex 2.0: Key Technical Details

## (1) Process-Reward Operator (PRO)

**Training Data & Scale:**
PRO is "pretrained in isolation on real executed trajectories from industrial deployment data, where ground-truth progress, risk, and termination signals are available from operational telemetry." The system trained on "a curated subset of 10 million interactions" from over 500 million total warehouse manipulation interactions collected at 30 Hz.

**What It Scores:**
PRO evaluates candidate rollouts using three criteria:
- **Progress**: "how much closer the predicted future brings the system to successful task completion"
- **Risk**: "probability of a failure event occurring along the imagined trajectory"
- **Termination**: "likelihood that the imagined trajectory leads to successful task completion"

These combine into: S_j = Δp^(j) - λρ^(j) + βd^(j)

## (2) Latent Space

PRO operates exclusively in **visual latent space**. It "consumes the sequence of predicted latents" generated by the world model and produces "rollout-level representation" for scoring. The authors note this design choice is critical because "imagined futures remain grounded in the same representational space as real observations."

## (3) Candidate Trajectories (k)

The paper evaluates k=2 as the primary "low-latency setting" for all task evaluations, though Figure 8 demonstrates a spectrum: success rate increases from 0.962 (k=1) to 0.996 (k=30), with inference time increasing from 310ms to 9,200ms respectively.

## (4) Training Data Scale

- **Deployment data**: >10M episodes, >25k hours
- **Teleoperation**: ~40k episodes, ~400 hours
- **Open-source**: ~970k episodes, ~2k hours
- **Synthetic**: ~20k episodes

## (5) Performance Numbers

Across four industrial tasks, Cortex 2.0 achieved:
- Pick-and-place: 0.98 success, 0 human interventions
- Sorting items/trash: 0.95 per-operation success, 0 interventions
- Screw sorting: 0.98 per-operation success, 0 interventions
- Shoebox unpacking: 0.96 success, 0 interventions

Human intervention requirement was zero across all benchmarks.
